title: Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition duyuruldu
summary: Ghost of Yōtei için yeni hikaye genişlemesi ve roguelike modu içeren Complete Edition duyuruldu.
body:
Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition duyuruldu ve oyunun hayranlarına hem yeni bir hikaye genişlemesi hem de roguelike mod sunmaya hazırlanıyor. Polygon ve VGC gibi kaynakların aktardığına göre bu yeni paket, oyunun ana karakteri Atsu'nun geçmişine odaklanan içeriklerle zenginleştirildi.

## Echoes of Sekigahara ve Most Wanted yenilikleri

Paketin en dikkat çekici kısmı olan **Echoes of Sekigahara** hikaye genişlemesi, Atsu'nun intikam yolculuğundan önceki dönemini ve geçmişindeki romantik ilişkilerini ele alıyor. Yaklaşık 5 süren ana kampanyanın yanı sıra yeni bir bölge, ağır silahlar ve okçuluk yetenekleri oyuna ekleniyor. Diğer yandan **Most Wanted** adlı roguelike mod ise oyuncuların düşman dalgalarına karşı mücadele etmesini sağlarken, Ghost of Tsushima'nın kahramanı Jin Sakai'yi de tekrar oynanabilir karakter olarak geri getiriyor.

## Savaş mekanikleri ve karakter derinliği

Erika Ishii'nin seslendirdiği Atsu karakterine yeni derinlikler kazandıran bu genişlemede, düşman okçuların yeni ok türleri ve tuzaklar gibi zorluklar da oyuncuları bekliyor. Sucker Punch imzalı yapım, görsel ve işitsel kalitesini korurken serinin hikayesini tamamlayıcı bir deneyim vadediyor.

**Neden önemli?** Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition, ana hikayede eksik kalan karakter detaylarını açığa çıkaran hikaye ekleri ve yeni oynanış modlarıyla oyunculara kapsamlı bir geri dönüş fırsatı sunuyor.

source_texts.title: Ghost of Yōtei’s New DLC Should Have Been in the Game from the Very Start
source_texts.summary: Ghost of Yotei's narrative-focused Echoes of Sekigahara expansion gives much-needed depth to Atsu, played by an excellent Erika Ishii.
source_texts.text:
In last year’s Ghost of Yōtei, player character Atsu is driven by one thing: revenge. Her journey to slaughter the Yōtei Six — masked murderers who killed her family and left her for dead as a child — plays out largely like you’d expect an old-fashioned revenge tale, with a few wrinkles along the way.
But she mostly remains static; a singular force hellbent on revenge at all costs. Ghost of Yōtei doesn’t explore the costs until near the end of Atsu’s journey. The game’s new expansion, Echoes of Sekigahara, does the opposite — it’s all about consequences as it adds new layers of depth to Atsu. In fact, it fleshes out her character so much that it’s almost a shame it wasn’t part of the game at launch and is instead an optional add-on 12 months later.
Life before the Onryō
Before returning to Ezo, Atsu was a wandering swordsman, killing for coin throughout southern Japan and acting as a soldier for different lords. One of her adventures found her serving Lord Ishida during the Battle of Sekigahara. She met Nagato the Handsome during this time, a commander of troops and a good marksman. (And quite the looker.)
The romantic chemistry between him and Atsu is obvious to start. During Nagato’s introduction scene, he teaches Atsu an archery technique by standing behind her and guiding her hands on the bow; it’s classic Romance Movie Writing 101 shit. But the simplicity works, and helps Atsu become more of a person, and not just a bloodthirsty ghost. She was once someone who had the capacity to romantically love another, even though her quest for vengeance was unfulfilled at the time.
Flashbacks throughout Echoes of Sekigahara’s narrative give more insight into the love between them. Before the Battle of Sekigahara, a softer Atsu than the one we know even envisions a future for her and Nagato together, away from her revenge quest. Of course, Ghost of Yōtei is all about that revenge quest, so you can guess where this goes. Their falling out is as tragic as any.
In the present day, Echoes of Sekigahara takes Atsu to a new region, the Ashoro Foothills, after she hears of a bounty on Nagato’s head there. Three years after Sekigahara, they cross paths. This time, the tension isn’t romantic; Atsu’s ready to cut him down right away. Instead, they work together to disrupt Lord Saito’s operations in the Ashoro Foothills.
Along the way, they contend with their actions in the past and their regrets. I can’t help but wonder where Atsu’s path would have taken her if she hadn’t been deeply wounded by Nagato. If she and Nagato hadn’t gone their separate ways, would the Onryō have ever existed? Or would life as a vengeful ghost always have been Atsu’s destiny, with a romance only being a temporary distraction?
All these conflicting feelings and flashbacks to a gentler Atsu give star Erika Ishii new opportunities to shine. They bring a subtle tenderness to Atsu in moments between her and Nagato, like when they share a hot spring together and ponder their future. They also get plenty of moments to tap into Atsu’s anger and thirst for revenge, too. Ishii was nominated for Best Performance at The Game Awards, and co-won the DICE award for Outstanding Achievement in Character, so their performance in Echoes of Sekigahara is a reminder why.
Revenge comes at a cost
In the Ashoro Foothills, Echoes of Sekigahara also explores the impact of Atsu’s revenge on those outside of her wolf pack. These lands used to be controlled by the Snake, the Yōtei Six member Atsu kills in the base game’s opening moments. His death didn’t bring the land peace or levity. Instead, places where he offered protection in exchange for goods and hospitality have now been ravaged by his gang of goons, called Vipers, with many vying for his now-open spot in Lord Saito’s gang. His absence has created a vacuum, and the worst of the worst are trying to fill it.
Atsu may have gained from the Snake’s death, but the same can’t be said for the people he used to live among. Echoes of Sakigahara makes it clear that this revenge quest has far reaching consequences on the regular, unnamed folk of Ezo. Atsu even crosses paths with someone who used to love the Snake, in their own way. That’s right — the drunk murderer who died atop Atsu was a person with multiple dimensions. Echoes of Sakigahara shows that even murderers can be mourned, too.
The poor animals suffer as well. Ghost of Yōtei revels in connecting the player to nature through sweeping shots of beautiful hills, views from atop mountains, and adorable foxes to pet. Echoes of Sakigahara is no different. There are even more animals to chill with, my favorite being a cute little bear cub who needs Atsu’s help.
But then I release from captivity a different bear cub later on, who immediately plops down next to its dead parent to whimper and mourn, and am reminded of how the vipers are devastating the wildlife of Ashoro Foothills all to feed Lord Saito’s army. They hunt endlessly, culling the wildlife population. We’re introduced to the Viper when they go after Atsu’s wolf companion, as if you need any more reason to eagerly cut the villains down.
New ways to slay
That wolf, whom I had named Mikage, shows up for just about every big fight, joining standoffs by Atsu’s side. A side quest involving Mikage can reward Atsu with pretty slick armor that switches one of her Spirit abilities to an attack that summons wolves to stagger an enemy, reflecting Atsu’s growing bond with the world around her.
Also new are heavy weapons Atsu can pick up and use until they break. She also gets an armor set later in the game that switches her attack to one where she can headshot three dudes at once with her bow. None of these additions change the flow of battle or duels much, but I won’t say no to new ways to quickly kill foes, especially considering that Ghost of Yōtei’s combat can grow rather rote after playing it for over 60 hours in total.
Echoes of Sekigahara’s best combat addition might be the way it makes your enemies tougher. Archers have a new arrow type that lodges in Atsu, forcing you to pull it out before you can heal or use Spirit for attacks. I’ll catch myself on the ropes sometimes, trying to find an opening to pull the arrow out. It’s especially tough when I get hit by one of those arrows in a duel as those opponents are fast and relentless, but I welcome some new challenges.
Even with those new bells and whistles, my favorite part of combat remains standoffs, just like in the base game. One-slashing enemies never gets old, especially when Mikage gets in on the fun. But I’m not playing Echoes of Sekigahara for its fights. The main draw here is its character work, which it excels at.
Open worlds may never lend themselves to protagonists with the most depth moment-to-moment, and Ghost of Yōtei is no different in that regard. By focusing on adding new layers to Atsu and exploring the ramifications of her actions, Echoes of Sekigahara shines in ways the base game didn’t.

source_texts.title: Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition review: An expansion worth returning for
source_texts.summary: Ghost of Yotei's new expansion is full of heart and violence, even if it's not as long as we'd like
source_texts.text:
There have never been more things competing for your time, and money.
More games than ever are released every day, infinite streaming services provide more content for less money than at any point in human history. Alongside that, you’re expected to work, feed yourself, and generally interact with the real people in your life.
That’s why I often find such friction when returning to a game I’ve not played in months, even if I loved it the first time around. Live service games are the biggest culprit of this, with virtually none of them adequately introducing re-onboarding measures for players who take a break.
However, when the new content is as good as that offered in Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition, it’s more than worth returning to Atsu’s journey, even if you’ve long-since popped the Platinum.
Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition is comprised of Most Wanted and Echoes of Sekigahara. The former is a roguelike mode which sees players take on waves of enemies before facing a member of the Yotei Six, and the latter is a story expansion.
Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition’s Most Wanted mode is a compelling take on the roguelike genre, and a worthwhile addition to a game that already boasted a substantial single-player and multiplayer offering.
In Most Wanted, the player is stripped down to the base abilities of each character, and is then tasked with taking on waves of tougher and tougher foes. Death is inevitable, and with each run the player earns currency they can use to purchase abilitlies, and unlock new playable characters.
The headline here is that this mode reintroduces Jin Sakai, the protagonist of Ghost of Tsushima, as a playable character. He’s joined by Atsu and two other playable heroes, each of which play slightly differently. The loop of completing rounds and being rewarded is satisfying, even if the curve for earning currency is a litte steep in the beginning.
Echoes of Sekigahara is the highlight of Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition. While not as large as the Iki Island expansion from the first game, the story it tells is one of the richest across the franchise.
Echoes of Sekigahara begins with Atsu hunting a bounty from her past. A samurai that she fought alongside in the war. The DLC includes flashbacks to Atsu’s time before she returned to Yotei and became the titular Ghost, and brings with it a new side to Atsu.
A new, smaller region is introduced in Echoes of Sekigahara, which includes new bounties, dye merchants, and more. It’s certainly more limited in scope than a full-on expansion, but what is there is all enjoyable. The main campaign will take around 5 hours to complete, with side missions and bounties adding a few extra hours on top.
Echoes of Sekigahara’s biggest addition is two new fighting mechanics: massive weapons and a new deadeye-style ability that allows Atsu to fire three arrows at once, each auto-targeting an enemy. Yotei already offered so many weapon types and gadgets that there were certainly some that I virtually never touched in the base game, but both of these new additions are welcome.
The massive weapons, which add a category to the skill tree, function like other weapon pickups from defeated enemies, though it’s possible to upgrade your skill with them and use them a few times before they break. These are fun for crowd busting, but they’re less agile and satisfying than picking up an enemy’s sword and Luke Littlering it across a rice field at them.
The world of Echoes of Sekigahara is now full of traps, and a new enemy type will shoot arrows deep into Atsu’s arm, which requires the player to remove it before they can heal or use any spirit abilities. It makes the region feel slightly different, even if combat encounters play out mostly the same as in the base game.
Echoes of Sekigahara’s strongest moments come in the main story missions, which are full of great writing, and another strong performance from Erika Ishii. Ishii’s portrayal of a younger Atsu, when compared to the Ghost she’d become, is very effective, and adds context to the character that makes me rather surprised this portion of her story was relegated to DLC.
The highest praise I can give Echoes of Sekigahara is that the main story of Ghost of Yotei is weaker without these sections. This is a “Complete Edition” that actually feels complete from a narrative perspective. I wish there was more of it, and this was a more Iki Island-sized adventure.
The great things about the base game remain, namely the best-in-class presentation. Ghost of Yotei’s excellent soundtrack, including the “chill beats to behead your enemies to” Wantanabe Mode, makes riding across this new chunk of Japan a joy.
The soundscape greatly complements visuals which can go toe-to-toe with any other game on the platform. Some of the shots of the landscape as Mount Yotei pierces the sun on the horizon are absurd.
I left Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition with a reaffirmed appreciation for the base game, and a desire to go back and do absolutely everything the island has to offer. The new expansion is strong enough that it should never have been divorced from the main narrative, and Most Wanted is another string to the game’s already content-rich bow.
If this is your first time picking up Sucker Punch‘s latest, what is here is one of the best “Complete Editions” of a game in a while, even if the new story content isn’t quite as long as I had hoped for. Though between the base game, Ghost of Yotei Legends, Most Wanted, and now Echoes of Sekigahara, it’s difficult to imagine you running out of things to do quickly.
Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition review
Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition is a perfect excuse to return to Atsu's story. Most Wanted is engaging and challenging, and the new story expansion is some of the best content across both the base game and DLC. It's a shame it isn't longer, but what is here is a vital new chapter in the Ghost's story.
- Echoes of Sekigahara's narrative is a great.
- The story revelations around Atsu's pre-Ghost life.
- The new region shines as the base game's presentational might remains.
- Most Wanted is a fun new mode in an already content-rich offering.
- It's not very long.
